sections: Centimetres to inches, the way you actually need it

Type a length in centimetres and get the answer three ways at once: as a decimal (66.929 in), as a fraction to the nearest sixteenth of an inch (66 15/16 in) – the way tape measures and rulers are marked – and in feet and inches (5 ft 6 15/16 in), the way heights are written in the US and UK. The converter also shows the formula with your number filled in, a table of the same length in every other unit (mm, m, km, ft, yd, mi), and a swap button for inches to centimetres.

One inch is defined as exactly **2.54 centimetres**. That definition has been international since 1959, so the conversion is exact – there is no rounding in the factor, only in how many decimals you choose to display.
To go the other way: **centimetres = inches × 2.54**.

For feet and inches: divide the total inches by 12. The whole number is feet; the remainder is inches. Example: 170 cm ÷ 2.54 = 66.93 in; 66.93 ÷ 12 = 5 remainder 6.93 → 5 ft 6.93 in (about 5 ft 7 in).
**30 cm** ÷ 2.54 = 11.81 in – just under a foot (a standard school ruler).
**55 cm** cabin bag = 21.65 in (often quoted as 22 in).
**2.5 cm** = 0.98 in – roughly one inch, handy for quick estimates.

For a quick estimate, multiply centimetres by 4 and divide by 10: 50 cm × 4 = 200 → 20 in (exact: 19.69 in). This overestimates by about 1.6%. To go from inches to centimetres, multiply by 2.5 and add a little: 10 in × 2.5 = 25 → 25.4 cm. For heights, remember that 152.4 cm is exactly 5 ft, and each extra inch adds 2.54 cm.

Imperial rulers and tape measures divide each inch into halves, quarters, eighths and sixteenths. The longest tick in the middle is 1/2; the next longest are 1/4 and 3/4; then the eighths (1/8, 3/8, 5/8, 7/8); and the shortest ticks are sixteenths. When the converter shows 66 15/16 in, look for the 66-inch mark and count fifteen of the smallest ticks beyond it – or, more simply, one tick before the 67-inch mark. A sixteenth of an inch is about 1.6 mm, which is the precision most woodworking, sewing and DIY projects need.
Where you meet cm and inches
A short history of the inch and the centimetre

The centimetre is one hundredth of a metre, the base unit of length in the International System of Units (SI). The metre was originally defined in 1793 as one ten-millionth of the distance from the North Pole to the equator, and since 1983 it has been defined by the distance light travels in a vacuum in 1/299,792,458 of a second. The inch has older roots: in many languages the word for inch also means thumb, and medieval English law defined it as the length of three barleycorns. Different countries' inches varied slightly until 1959, when the United States, United Kingdom, Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa agreed on the international inch of exactly 25.4 millimetres. Today almost every country uses centimetres for everyday measurements, while the United States – and the UK for some uses such as heights and screen sizes – still commonly uses inches.

Because 1 in = 2.54 cm exactly, the only error comes from rounding the result. For most purposes, two decimal places of an inch (0.01 in ≈ 0.25 mm) are more than enough. Engineering drawings often use three decimals (thousandths of an inch, 'thou'). For woodworking and sewing, the nearest 1/16 in is standard; for heights, the nearest whole inch. The converter shows up to eight significant decimals so you can round to whatever your project requires.

sections: Kilograms to pounds – plus ounces and stone

Enter a weight in kilograms and see it in pounds straight away – and, because a decimal like 154.32 lb isn't how people talk about weight, also in **pounds and ounces** (154 lb 5.2 oz) and in **stone and pounds** (11 st 0.3 lb), the form used for body weight in the UK and Ireland. The result updates as you type, shows the formula with your number, and lists the weight in grams, ounces, tonnes, tola and quintal too. Swap to convert pounds to kilograms.

The pound is defined as exactly **0.45359237 kg**, so 1 kg = 2.20462262 lb. The converter uses the exact definition, not a rounded factor, so results stay correct even for large values such as freight weights in tonnes.
**Ounces:** take the decimal part of the pounds and multiply by 16. **Stone:** divide pounds by 14; the whole number is stone, the remainder pounds.

Double the kilograms and add 10%: 70 kg → 140 + 14 = 154 lb (exact 154.3). Going back, halve the pounds and subtract 10%: 200 lb → 100 − 10 = 90 kg (exact 90.7). This is accurate to within about 0.5%.

Doctors, gyms and fitness apps in most countries record weight in kilograms; in the US it is pounds, and in the UK and Ireland people often say stone and pounds. A body weight of 60 kg is 132.3 lb or 9 st 6.3 lb; 75 kg is 165.3 lb or 11 st 11.3 lb; 90 kg is 198.4 lb or 14 st 2.4 lb. For a BMI calculation, use kilograms and metres – our [BMI calculator](/bmi-calculator/) accepts both systems.

sections: Airlines set their own limits and change them, so always check your ticket. Note that 23 kg is slightly more than 50 lb, which is why the two are used interchangeably.
**Recipes:** 1 lb of flour or meat = 453.6 g; 500 g ≈ 1.1 lb; 250 g ≈ 8.8 oz.
**Gym plates:** a 20 kg barbell = 44.1 lb; 45 lb plates = 20.4 kg.
**Parcels:** postal services price by weight bands; 2 kg = 4.41 lb, 5 kg = 11.02 lb.
**Babies:** a 3.5 kg newborn weighs 7 lb 11.5 oz.
**Produce:** 1 kg of apples is about 2.2 lb.

The **kilogram** is the SI base unit of mass. Since 2019 it has been defined by fixing the Planck constant, replacing the platinum-iridium cylinder kept near Paris that served as the standard for 130 years. The **pound** (abbreviated lb, from the Latin libra) is used in the United States and, alongside kilograms, in the UK; the international avoirdupois pound was fixed at exactly 0.45359237 kg in 1959. A pound has 16 **ounces** (oz), and 14 pounds make a **stone** (st), a unit still common for body weight in Britain and Ireland. In India, the **tola** (11.66 g) is used for gold, and the **quintal** (100 kg) for crops.

Strictly, kilograms and pounds measure mass – the amount of matter – while weight is the force of gravity on that mass. In everyday life the words are used interchangeably, and bathroom scales are calibrated to show mass. On the Moon your mass in kilograms would be the same, but scales calibrated for Earth would show about a sixth of it.

Many recipes from the US list ingredients in pounds and ounces, while European and Indian recipes use grams and kilograms. 1 kg is 2 lb 3.3 oz; half a kilo (500 g) is 1 lb 1.6 oz; 100 g is 3.5 oz; and 1 oz is 28.35 g. For baking, where accuracy matters, weigh in grams if your scale allows – it avoids the rounding that comes with fractions of ounces. Nutrition labels in the US show serving sizes in both ounces and grams, while energy is shown in calories; our [unit converter](/unit-converter/) also converts kcal to kJ.
Rounding: how precise should you be?

For body weight, one decimal place in kilograms or a whole pound is plenty – your weight changes by more than that during a day. For luggage, round down to be safe: 23 kg is 50.7 lb, so a bag showing 50 lb on an American scale is within the limit. For shipping, round up to the next weight band. For medicine dosages and laboratory work, use the full precision shown and follow the instructions of a professional.

seo.title: Celsius to Fahrenheit – °C to °F Formula, Chart, Kelvin
seo.desc: Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit instantly with the formula shown for your number, plus Kelvin. Shortcut, −40 to 250 °C chart, body and oven temps.
seo.compareTitle: {tool}: {brand} vs RapidTables, Inch Calculator and Metric-Conversions
sections: Type a temperature in Celsius and get Fahrenheit immediately, with the calculation written out using your number – °F = 37 × 1.8 + 32 = 98.6 – and the same temperature in Kelvin. Swap to convert Fahrenheit to Celsius. Below the converter you'll find a reference chart from −40 °C to 250 °C and the temperatures people look up most: fever, weather, cooking and ovens.

Why 9/5 and 32? Water freezes at 0 °C = 32 °F and boils at 100 °C = 212 °F. The 100 Celsius degrees between those points span 180 Fahrenheit degrees, so one Celsius degree is 1.8 Fahrenheit degrees, and the scales are offset by 32.

**Double it and add 30.** 20 °C → 40 + 30 = 70 °F (exact 68). It is within 2–3 °F for everyday weather between 0 and 30 °C. For the reverse, **subtract 30 and halve**: 80 °F → 50 ÷ 2 = 25 °C (exact 26.7). A handy rhyme for weather: 'Thirty is hot, twenty is nice, ten is chilly, zero is ice.'

A normal body temperature is around 37 °C (98.6 °F), although healthy values vary between about 36.1 and 37.2 °C (97 to 99 °F) depending on the person, the time of day and where it is measured. A temperature of 38 °C (100.4 °F) or above is generally considered a fever. Always follow medical advice for your situation; this converter only translates the numbers.
Recipes usually round oven temperatures: 180 °C is printed as 350 °F (exact 356 °F). For fan (convection) ovens, reduce the temperature by about 20 °C (25 °F).

Almost every country uses Celsius for weather, cooking and medicine. The United States, its territories, and a few other countries such as the Bahamas, Belize, the Cayman Islands and Liberia use Fahrenheit for everyday temperatures. Scientists everywhere use Celsius and Kelvin. The Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero, the lowest possible temperature, and uses the same step size as Celsius; it has no degree symbol – you write 300 K, not 300 °K.

If you travel between the US and the rest of the world, it helps to memorise a few anchor points: 10 °C = 50 °F (jacket weather), 20 °C = 68 °F (pleasant), 25 °C = 77 °F (warm), 30 °C = 86 °F (hot) and 40 °C = 104 °F (extreme heat). For cold weather, remember that −18 °C is about 0 °F and −40 is the same on both scales.

seo.title: IST to EST Converter – Auto EDT/DST, Overlap Hours
seo.desc: Convert India Standard Time to US Eastern Time with automatic EST/EDT daylight saving, a working-hours overlap grid, next clock change and shareable links.
sections: IST to Eastern Time, with daylight saving handled for you

Pick a date and time in India Standard Time and see it instantly in New York (US Eastern Time), London (or any zone you choose), with an hour-by-hour table for the whole day that highlights everyone's 9-to-5 working hours. The converter knows that the US Eastern zone switches between **EST (UTC−5)** in winter and **EDT (UTC−4)** in summer, so the difference from India changes from 10 h 30 min to 9 h 30 min – and it tells you when the next clock change happens.

Share a meeting time with one click: 'Copy link' creates a URL that opens the converter with your exact date, time and zones, so colleagues see it in their own time zones. The conversion uses your browser's built-in time-zone database (the same IANA database used by phones and operating systems).

India does not use daylight saving time, so all the change comes from the US side. US clocks go forward at 2:00 am local time on the second Sunday in March and back at 2:00 am on the first Sunday in November. In 2026 that means EDT until **1 November 2026**, then EST until **14 March 2027**.
How to convert IST to EST by hand
**Winter (EST):** subtract 10 hours 30 minutes from IST. 7:30 pm IST → 9:00 am EST.
**Summer (EDT):** subtract 9 hours 30 minutes. 7:30 pm IST → 10:00 am EDT.
If the result is negative, add 24 hours and it's the previous day in the US. 6:00 am IST Tuesday → 7:30 pm EST Monday.
Best meeting times between India and the US East Coast

The 9:00–17:00 working days in India and New York do not overlap at all. The usual compromise is the Indian evening and the American morning: **7:30–9:30 pm IST = 9:00–11:00 am EST** (or 10:00 am–12:00 pm EDT). Teams that prefer Indian mornings meet at **8:00–9:00 am IST**, which is 9:30–10:30 pm EST the previous evening. The hour-by-hour grid in the converter shows these options for any date, and highlights rows where all chosen zones are within working hours.
What do IST, EST, EDT and ET mean?
**IST – India Standard Time:** UTC+5:30, used across all of India all year. (IST can also mean Irish or Israel Standard Time in other contexts.)
**EST – Eastern Standard Time:** UTC−5, US East Coast in winter (New York, Washington, Miami, Atlanta, Boston, Toronto).
**EDT – Eastern Daylight Time:** UTC−4, the same places in summer.
**ET – Eastern Time:** the general name for whichever of EST/EDT applies. Many people say 'EST' all year; the converter shows the correct one for your date.
**UTC:** Coordinated Universal Time, the world reference time.

Choose up to three target zones from the full list of world time zones – for example Chicago (Central Time, IST −11:30/−10:30), Los Angeles (Pacific Time, IST −13:30/−12:30), London, Dubai or Singapore. Daylight-saving rules for every zone are applied automatically, including the weeks in March and October/November when the US and Europe change clocks on different dates.

The converter runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you type is sent anywhere, there is no tracking of your values, and once the page has loaded it keeps working offline – handy on a building site, in a shop or on a plane.
